title: Rinderpest in Africa
body: In the late nineteenth century, Europeans came to Africa hoping to set up plantations and mines, but few Africans were willing to work for wages, since land and livestock sustained their livelihoods. Employers imposed heavy taxes that could be paid only by working on plantations and mines, and changed inheritance laws so that only one member of a family could inherit land. Then, in the late 1880s, rinderpest arrived, carried by infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers invading Eritrea. It moved west 'like forest fire', reaching the Atlantic coast in 1892 and the Cape five years later, and killed 90 per cent of the cattle along the way. Planters, mine owners and colonial governments then took control of the scarce cattle that remained.

title: The depression in Bengal and in Indian towns
body: In Bengal, peasants grew raw jute that was processed in factories into gunny bags for export. When gunny exports collapsed during the Great Depression, the price of raw jute crashed by more than 60 per cent. Peasants who had borrowed in the hope of better times, or to grow more in the hope of higher incomes, faced ever lower prices and fell deeper into debt. Although agricultural prices fell sharply, the colonial government refused to reduce its revenue demand. A song of the jute growers warned that after all their spending, traders sitting at home would pay them only a few rupees a maund. In the towns, things looked different. People with fixed incomes, such as landowners receiving rents and middle-class salaried employees, found that everything now cost less.
